name: Cysteamine
lead: Cysteamine (2-aminoethanethiol, mercaptamine) is a small organosulfur compound containing both an amine and a thiol group. It is made naturally in mammals during the breakdown of coenzyme A and is used as a medicine for nephropathic cystinosis, a lysosomal storage disease in which cystine accumulates in cells.[1]

In dermatology, a topical cysteamine preparation is used to lighten skin darkened by melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or sun exposure, and is described as a non-hydroquinone option.[1][2][3] A 2025 double-blind randomized trial compared an overnight leave-on cream containing 5 percent cysteamine and ectoine with 4 percent hydroquinone cream in melasma.[4]

Dermatology reviews list cysteamine hydrochloride among oral and topical agents used for hyperpigmentation, while noting that treatments for pigmentation often take long to work and carry adverse effects.[3] A practical limit noted in a general reference is instability of the molecule, which oxidizes in air to cystamine.[5]

paras: Topical cysteamine is used for melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and sun-related dark spots.[1][2] Reviews of topical melasma treatment and hyperpigmentation management list it among agents beyond hydroquinone and triple combination cream, which remain the best-studied options.[2][3]

Cysteamine is indicated for cystinosis under the brand names Cystagon and Procysbi and as eye drops; the US label for the ophthalmic product (Cystadrops) lists treatment of corneal cystine crystal deposits in adults and children with cystinosis.[1][6] The first report of benefit in cystinosis dates to the 1950s, and a 1987 trial in children established therapy for nephropathic cystinosis.[1][7] It has also been studied for Huntington's disease, mitochondrial disease, cystic fibrosis, fatty liver disease and depression, and in the past as an antidote for paracetamol overdose.[8][9][10][11][12][13]

For hyperpigmentation, the main controlled evidence is the 2025 multicenter double-blind randomized comparison of 5 percent cysteamine with ectoine against 4 percent hydroquinone in melasma.[4] A review of topical melasma treatments reports that triple combination therapy and hydroquinone remain the most well-studied agents with strong evidence-based recommendations, with several other agents having evidence of effectiveness.[2] Published trials of topical cysteamine are modest in size relative to hydroquinone.

The 2025 randomized trial compared an overnight leave-on cysteamine and ectoine cream with 4 percent hydroquinone in melasma.[4] Reviews summarise topical melasma and hyperpigmentation therapies.[2][3]

Outside pigmentation, clinical studies include a 1987 trial of cysteamine in children with nephropathic cystinosis,[7] pharmacokinetic work in cystinosis patients,[14] enteric-coated bitartrate studies,[15] a 2017 randomized placebo-controlled trial in 96 patients with early Huntington's disease,[8] registered trials in cystinosis, mitochondrial disease, cystic fibrosis, fatty liver in children and major depression,[9][10][11][12][13][16][17] and a 2026 gene therapy study in cystinosis in which oral cysteamine was withdrawn before infusion.[18]

Wikipedia reports that oral cysteamine labels warn of Ehlers-Danlos-like symptoms, severe skin rashes, gastrointestinal ulcers or bleeding, central nervous system effects including seizures and encephalopathy, low white blood cell counts and idiopathic intracranial hypertension, with bad breath, skin odor, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain also reported.[1] The eye drop label lists eye pain, blurred vision, irritation, redness and ocular deposits as the most common effects and warns about benign intracranial hypertension reported with oral use.[6] The label notes teratogenicity in rats at oral doses 240 to 960 times the human ophthalmic dose and says adequate human data are lacking.[6]
For topical skin use, the sources reviewed describe odor and instability as practical drawbacks but give no detailed adverse event rates.

In cystinosis, cysteamine enters lysosomes and converts cystine into cysteine and a cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide, both of which can leave the lysosome.[1][6] The mechanism in skin is described in the dermatology reviews as involving tyrosinase and related inhibition and antioxidant activity; the sources reviewed here do not give a detailed account.[3]

Cysteamine has the formula HSCH2CH2NH2 and is a water-soluble white solid, often used as the hydrochloride or bitartrate. It oxidizes in air to the disulfide cystamine, which complicates formulation.[1][5]

The therapeutic effect on cystinosis was reported in the 1950s; the US approved cysteamine for cystinosis in 1994 and an extended-release form in 2013.[1] A 1977 review noted that intravenous cysteamine appeared effective in preventing liver damage from acetaminophen overdose if given within about ten hours, and a history of paracetamol poisoning discusses early antidotes.[19][20]
The forum sources reviewed contain no discussion of cysteamine for appearance.

timeline.event: Therapeutic effect of cysteamine on cystinosis reported.[1]
